ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in $\triangle ABC$, $\angle ABC=90^\circ$, circle $\odot O$ with diameter $AB$ intersects $AC$ at point $D$, $AE$ is perpendicular to the tangent at point $D$, with the foot of the perpendicular being $E$. $AD$ bisects $\angle BAE$; If $CD=\frac{9}{5}$ and $BC=3$, find the length of segment $AB$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Connect BD, as shown in the figure,

$\because$ AB is a diameter,

$\therefore$ $\angle$ADB$=90^\circ$,

$\because$ $\angle 2+\angle$ABD$=90^\circ$, $\angle 3+\angle$ABD$=90^\circ$,

$\therefore$ $\angle 2=\angle 3$,

$\because$ $\angle$DCB$=\angle$BCA,

$\therefore$ $\triangle CDB\sim \triangle CBA$,

$\therefore$ $\frac{CD}{CB}=\frac{CB}{AC}$,

$\therefore$ $\frac{\frac{9}{5}}{3}=\frac{3}{AC}$,

$\therefore$ AC$=5$,

$\therefore$ AB$=\sqrt{AC^2-BC^2}=\sqrt{5^2-3^2}=\boxed{4}$

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, AB is the horizontal diameter of the circle, and O is on AB; point B is at the right end of the circle, BC goes vertically upward from point B and is perpendicular to AB; the oblique line AC extends from A through D on the circle to C, so viewed from the external point C, C-D-A is a secant line. The tangent line at point D and AE perpendicular to that tangent line are also drawn in the figure, but this method mainly uses the tangent relationship at point B. Reasoning: Because OB is on the diameter AB, and BC\perp AB, BC is also perpendicular to the radius OB. Therefore BC is the tangent line to the circle at point B. The tangent drawn from the external point C is CB, and the secant line is C-D-A. By the tangent-secant theorem, CB^2=CD\cdot CA. Substituting CB=3, CD=\frac{9}{5}, we get 3^2=\frac{9}{5}\cdot CA, so CA=\frac{9}{9/5}=5. Also because \angle ABC=90^\circ, in the right triangle ABC, AB=\sqrt{AC^2-BC^2}=\sqrt{5^2-3^2}=\sqrt{16}=4.
